newsitem.title: USA: Isuzu sues Consumers Union over Trooper story.
newsitem.headline: Isuzu sues Consumers Union over Trooper story.

text.p: Isuzu Motors Ltd. Thursday filed a multimillion-dollar defamation suit against the publisher of Consumer Reports, claiming the magazine deliberately lied about the safety of Isuzu's flagship Trooper sport-utility vehicle.
The lawsuit, filed in federal district court here, marks the second time a Japanese automaker has challenged the testing methods of the popular consumer watchdog magazine.

Suzuki Motor Corp. has also accused Consumers Union of biased testing. In April, Suzuki claimed Consumers Union rigged a 1988 swerve test to make the Suzuki Samurai tip on two wheels in an effort to boost sales of its magazine.
A California judge recently dismissed all libel claims and product disparagement claims against Consumers Union by Suzuki but allowed the automaker's claim of deceptive trade practices to continue.

At a news conference here, Isuzu officials claimed Consumer Reports' test drivers "manhandled" the Trooper during a series of staged tests last summer to create dramatic video footage and photographs that would alarm the public.
"If you ever caught your kid driving that way, you'd send him to bed without supper, you'd spank him and you'd take away his keys for a month," said Richard Bowman, an attorney for Isuzu.
In a statement, Consumers Union said it stands by its tests.

"The issue here is consumer safety," the magazine's publishers said. "We haven't seen the legal complaint but we have heard the wild statements and false accusations at Isuzu's press conference. Isuzu's assertions were unjustified in every respect. We will prove that fully and unhesitatingly."

Bowman said the test drivers steered the Trooper in a manner "so radical, so extreme, so bizarre that no ordinary person would ever drive, or, for that matter, could ever drive that way in the real world."
Moreover, he claimed videotapes of earlier tests by Consumers Union showed drivers unable to tip the vehicle with one driver commenting: "It just slides."
Asked if he wanted to repeat the test again, the driver responded: "I don't see any point."

Consumer Reports, which rates a wide array of consumer products, is regarded as one of the most informative consumer safety publications because of its objective testing methods and long-standing policy for not taking advertising.
Consumer Reports said of the 61 vehicles tested over the years by its drivers, only two tipped over -- the 1988 Samurai and the 1995-96 Trooper, which is also sold as the Acura SLX.

Terry Maloney, senior vice president and general manager of Isuzu's light vehicles, said the automaker tried repeatedly to get the magazine to retract the August 1996 article, but the magazine's editors would not agree even after the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration denied Consumers Union's petition for a defect investigation of the Trooper.
"The Isuzu Trooper is a safe vehicle," Maloney said. "Consumers Union knew this when they originally recommended the 1995 and the 1996 Trooper in their Annual Car Guides."

"They knew it when they deliberately manipulated a Trooper to cause a tip-up in their so-called test in June of last year. They knew it when they first published the results of their so-called test last August, and every time they kept repeating their false statements about Isuzu and our Trooper. And they most certainly know it today, as they continue their pattern of disparagement and defamation even after NHTSA's denial of their petition," he added.
Bowman said the company is seeking compensatory and punitive damages against Consumers Union, publisher of Consumer Reports, and its technical director, David Pittle.

Bowman declined to say how much money Isuzu would seek but said it could easily stretch into the "many millions of dollars" and, if successful would be one of the biggest jury awards against a publication for an automaker.

Maloney said sales of the Trooper, a sport utility vehicle that competes with the Ford Explorer, Jeep Grand Cherokee and Chevrolet Blazer, were down 54 percent in the first six months of this year, largely as a result of the publicity surrounding the Consumer Reports article.
Isuzu said it will also request Consumers Union to turn over all its secret files on its tests, including videotapes and drivers' logs.
